KEY MESSAGE 1...Heavy rainfall is possible this afternoon and 
evening, mainly south of I-66, before turning quieter into
Tuesday.

A cold front is currently on the move as it edges south of
I-66/U.S. 50. The latest KLWX WSR-88 radar imagery shows a
broken line of storms moving well south/east of the Capital 
Beltway back down toward the central Virginia Piedmont and I-64 
corridor. Although some of these cells continue to pulse up, the
overall severe risk appears on the lower end as multiple gust 
fronts/outflows race out ahead. As of the mid-afternoon hours, 
the most consolidated area of showers and embedded thunderstorms
continues over Albemarle, Orange, and Spotsylvania counties in 
central Virginia. With a bulk of this area in a severe/extreme 
(D2-D3) drought, it will likely take quite a bit of torrential 
rainfall to flood. All of this convection is forecast to 
continue nosing south and east before exiting the entire 
forecast area by the early evening.

For areas to the north of the convection, skies have cleared out
rather quickly. A few local exceptions are noted as anvil cirrus
lift northeastward to near the metro areas. This drying effect 
is evident on the multi-channel water vapor imagery as the mean
longwave trough axis passes through. While the stronger forcing
is displaced well to the north into upstate New York and 
southern Quebec, enough height falls cross the local area to 
push this front through. By late this evening, the cold front is
expected to span southeastern Virginia back across interior
North Carolina. The post-frontal air mass will remain dry with
decreasing cloud cover. 

After spending much of the day in the low/mid 80s, expect 
temperatures and dew points to fall into tonight. With high
pressure building in from the upper Ohio Valley, forecast lows
are to fall into the upper 50s to 60s. For the Alleghenies, some
locations could even push into the mid 50s. The Shenandoah
Valley westward may see some patchy fog for locations that fully
decouple overnight under clear skies and light winds.

During subsequent days through mid-week, expect more tranquil
weather to arrive on Tuesday. High pressure remains in charge as
the stalled front sticks closer to the Virginia Tidewater
region. Clouds increase from the south as moisture overruns the
frontal system to the south. Despite the clouds, forecast highs
push back into the 80s, but with lower humidity levels.
Seasonable conditions persist into Tuesday night while a few
showers approach from central Virginia and the Northern Neck of
Virginia.

Wednesday yields the next shot for showers and thunderstorms. At
the synoptic level, a cut-off low over the southeastern U.S.
weakens/shears while subtropical ridging retrogrades toward the
Atlantic coast. As this occurs, mid-level winds begin to
increase along the western flank of the offshore anticyclone. A
series of perturbations in the flow will lift across the area at
the same time the surface front returns to the I-95 corridor.
Precipitable water values shift back to over 2 inches which will
not only increase humidity levels, but also bring heavy rainfall
back to the forecast. A Marginal Risk for excessive rainfall
exists on Wednesday as this pattern shift unfolds. Highs remain
in the 80s with afternoon heat indices into the mid 90s.


KEY MESSAGE 2: Increased shower and thunderstorm chances
Thursday into early next week.

Synoptically, we are still monitoring the progression of an upper 
level low pressure system over the Ohio River Valley/central 
Appalachians. This system will be slow to push eastward heading into 
the weekend and early next week. At the surface, is a 
stalled/washed out boundary that will act as a catalyst for several 
pieces of shortwave energy to move along yielding increased chances 
for showers and thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening 
periods each day. 

Additional showers and thunderstorms are likely Thursday through 
Sunday given the boundary washing out over the area. The warm/moist 
airmass combined with the washed out boundary and ripples of 
shortwave energy will aid in scattered to numerous diurnal 
thunderstorm development. Severe weather could be a concern each 
day, but overall confidence remains uncertain due to abundant cloud 
cover and no real forcing mechanisms. Expect much of the convection 
to be driven by terrain circulations or bay/river breeze 
interactions. Current machine learning probabilities remain between 
15-30 percent Thursday through Monday with 30-45 percent 
probabilities east of the Blue Ridge Friday. Friday may be the day 
where we have a more pronounced severe threat due to a lee side 
trough combined with 30-40kt mid level flow driving convection 
eastward. Locally damaging wind gusts will be the primary threat 
with storms along with isolated instances of flash flooding.
